title: The Tally Card
passages:
Nour pressed the grease pencil to the board ledge. The metal was cold under her palm, and her fingers left black smudges on the steel. She drew the first run: Anza to Culvert Nine, six cases of cornmeal, receiving mark Br-4. She left a space and drew the second.

"Six cases cornmeal," Teodoro said, reading over her shoulder. "Br-4. That's Odessa Brill's mark. Culvert Nine pump station. She used to take our overflow before Anza went red."

Nour didn't answer. She drew the second line.

"Second run. Four cases of fuse wire. Br-4 again. You're sending wire to a dead pump station while the node's on half rations."

"Read and don't talk," Nour said.

"Third run. Two cases of canned milk. Br-4. Fourth run..." He stopped. Nour's hand had started to shake. She dragged the pencil across the ledger, scoring a thick wrong line before she could lift it.

"Fourth run," Teodoro said, quieter now. "Six cases of respirator scrubbers. Receiving mark Br-4. Canisters, Nour. The same ones caged under Rhea's brother's cot. Six cases of them riding in Odessa Brill's hoard at the end of the ore line while Ivo burns through his last cartridge in the shop."

Nour looked up. Her grease pencil snapped in two.

"Rhea's pumping him by hand," she said. "One cartridge left. Fenn put the relay shop on brown-out."

"Six cases of scrubbers means Ivo could run for weeks. Why didn't you tell me where the seals went before I had to pull Culvert Nine off a dead rig at post 71?"

"Because keeping my head down is wisdom," Nour said. "And because Brill burned once. Now she trusts a full storeroom over any person's promise. She doesn't hand anything over without a trade."

Teodoro wiped his hands on his rag. "So we don't trade her food. We trade her the scrubbers. Or we take them back."

"If we take them, Anza eats canisters and still starves. If we trade, she keeps the hoard and we get six cases of canisters and a promise from a woman who doesn't make promises."

"The scrubbers *are* the trade," Teodoro said. "Ivo needs them. The node needs the eleven seals cleaned. Culvert Nine is where the skim lives. You drew the map. Now you walk it."

Outside, the ore siding groaned. A ghost train cycled its couplers, a sound like bones in a tin can. Nour stared at the fourth line. Six cases. The same part number stamped on Ivo's cage. Brill had them, and Nour had put them there.

"When do we leave?" she asked.

"First light," Teodoro said. "If Fenn doesn't serve the warrant first."

Nour broke the second piece of pencil and drew a circle around Culvert Nine.

The relay shop smelled of hot oil and old dust. Rhea’s arm ached from the bulb, the rubber tired and stubborn in her fist. Ivo lay on the cot behind the compressor, chest barely moving under the thin blanket. His respirator sat on the stool between them, its diaphragm patched with a disc of heavy glove rubber, the last cartridge screwed into the intake and hissing faintly with every cycle.

Fenn stood by the door, arms crossed, looking clean and unimpressed in their line-trust coat. Across the shop, the serve order was still taped to Marlowe’s bunk, but Fenn had come here anyway.

“Sign the release,” Fenn said. “Compressor priority restored the hour you do. Full power, no brown-out. Ivo gets his machine back.”

Rhea didn’t look up from the bulb. “Your offer can rot.”

Fenn’s jaw tightened. “You’re choosing a dead man’s name over your brother’s breath.”

“I’m choosing neither,” Rhea said. She squeezed. One, two, three hard pushes. Ivo’s chest lifted, shallow but real. She stopped before his eyes fluttered. “Teodoro. You learn this. Three pushes, watch the chest, stop before the eyes go. Too much air and you flood him. Too little and he doesn’t wake. You get a feel for the weight.”

Teodoro wiped grease from his hands onto his rag and crouched beside the cot. “And if I squeeze too long?”

“Then you’re killing him faster than the brown-out would.” Rhea slapped the wall beside the bench. A square of chalkboard paint had been scuffed there by years of shift notes. She found a nub of chalk and wrote a heavy 5. “Five restarts left in this cartridge. Five times I can squeeze enough air into his lungs to keep the canister working. Then the compressor spools up, seals against the glove-rubber patch, and eats a quarter of what remains just to build pressure.”

The machine groaned to life. The compressor cycled, and the cartridge gauge dipped. Rhea watched the needle fall a quarter turn. She wiped the chalk with her sleeve and wrote 4.

Fenn stepped closer. “Four restarts. Then what? You hand-pump him all night?”

“Then I find another way,” Rhea said. She didn’t look at them. “And you find another leverage.”

The compressor cycled again. Ivo’s breath hitched, then steadied. Fenn’s footsteps moved toward the door but stopped there, hand on the frame.

“First light,” Fenn said. “The warrant serves then. Whether you sign or not.”

Rhea sat down on the stool, her palm stinging from the bulb, and wrapped her hand around Ivo’s wrist. His pulse was thready under her thumb, but it was there.

She squeezed the bulb once, gently, and watched his chest rise. The needle on the cartridge gauge kept falling. Four restarts left, and the number on the wall was the only thing standing between Ivo and the dark.

Ospina worked the chipped die out of their coat and held it under the bay's work light. A seal die was a stamp — you pressed it into a cargo plate and it left a ring that said the load had been counted, sealed, and cleared to move. This one had a bite torn out of one edge, so every mark it made came up with a gap in the ring. They had pulled it from the med rig's tool void and never once pressed it to anything. Their own die had done the countersign that put Marlowe on Anza's plate as living crew — the real die, live authority, Shift 2, logged to their name at Kettering. That was the whole size of the trouble. The clean stamp had saved a man and flagged the hand that held it.

They dropped the chipped one back in their pocket. Evidence, or a paperweight, depending who asked.

"I'll walk down-line," Ospina said. "Whatever the crew drags back out of Culvert Nine, I'll seal it at the stub before it crosses the plate. Clean ring, my authority, chain complete. Anza eats on a legal load instead of a stolen one."

Boots first, though. Their bench boots were at Kettering, under the bench, where they were supposed to be standing at 08:00 when the morning desk opened the review on their flagged authority. A seal authority at their bench answers questions. A seal authority three nodes down the ore line at 08:00 has run.

Fenn was in the bay doorway. Ospina hadn't heard them come.

"You know what 08:00 is," Fenn said.

"I know what it is."

"Then you know a loader not standing at their bench when the review opens doesn't read as busy. It reads as flight." Fenn came a step in, coat still buttoned to the throat. "And flight changes the paper. Right now you're a review — a flag, a desk, a morning, some questions you might talk your way out of. You walk down-line and the flag becomes a warrant. Same name, different teeth. They don't ask you anything then. They come get you."

"Down-line first. Warrant after." Ospina spread their empty hands. "I've read the order of operations."

"You're doing it backwards."

"I'm doing it in the order that feeds the node." Ospina let the hands drop. "You want the eleven seals clean. Clean needs a chain — a counter at Bay 4, a seal at the receiving end. I'm the seal at the receiving end. There isn't another live authority this side of Kettering that'll touch a red plate. You haul that food home without me and it's still stolen when it lands. Anza starves on a technicality while I sit at a bench answering questions."

Fenn looked at them the way they looked at everything, a line that hadn't balanced.

"The desk will have your name by mid-morning," Fenn said.

"The desk's had my name for years." Ospina turned for the boot locker at the end of the bay. "It just never had a reason to walk it down a hallway."

The locker door was steel, the shift roster chalked on the front. Ospina's name sat under Shift 2. They didn't look at it. They pulled the door open and took their down-line boots off the bottom shelf, stiff with old grease, the laces fused at the eyelets, and sat on the bench to work the knots loose.

"You could stay," Fenn said, quieter now. "Stand the review. Keep the authority. That's a clean record if you keep it."

"A clean record doesn't breathe." Ospina got one boot on and stamped the heel down. "Tell Rhea the compressor's a piece of garbage and to save her four restarts for herself."

"Tell her yourself."

"She's busy." Ospina laced the second boot, slow, the grease giving up the knot one turn at a time. The bay clock over the door read a little past two. Six hours to 08:00, and every one of them about to be spent walking the wrong way from a bench that would have kept them clean.

They stood. They were taller in the boots, and the die rode in one pocket and their own live stamp in the other, and behind them a line-trust officer with a spotless record watched a loader choose the node.

"Log me out," Ospina said. "Down-line, seal authority, one die. If the desk calls before I'm back, tell them I'm working."

"I don't log people out of what they're running from."

"Then don't log me at all." Ospina walked past them into the yard. "A man with no line isn't a man who left."

Fenn didn't answer. The bay clock ticked past two. Ospina crossed the plate steel toward the ore line and the six hours between now and a warrant, carrying a stamp in each pocket — the clean one that would seal the food, and the chipped one they would never press.

Doan sat on the ore stub with their left wrist looped in the locker cord. The steel cable had been there since the clearance cut, biting into their sleeve every time they moved their hand. They pulled the seal knife from their belt — a short hooked blade meant for cutting cargo bands, not people — and sawed at the cord where it knotted around their wrist. It took three passes. The cord snapped, and Doan shook their hand until the feeling came back.

"Clearance withdrawn," they said. "Plate cold. Key dead. I'm a ghost with a locker."

Nour stood at the edge of the stub, arms crossed, her breath white in the cold. "We need you to walk the disused resupply route. On foot. Unlogged. Fenn froze the ore chute, so nothing can haul out of Anza until morning. If we're taking the hand cart down-line, we need someone who knows where the route runs under the snow."

Doan looked at Nour. "You want me to guide a crew down a route that doesn't exist on the board, carrying cargo that doesn't exist on a plate, with a clearance that doesn't exist anymore."

"That's the job," Nour said.

Doan stood, rubbing their wrist. "My price. No plates. No names. And everybody pushes the hand cart — you, me, Ospina, Miko if she shows. I don't carry dead weight for a node that already wrote me off."

"Agreed," Nour said.

Doan reached into their coat and pulled out nothing. The overlap log wasn't there — Miko held it, folded with her coast tickets. Instead, Doan looked up at the roster chalked on the ore stub wall, the names and shifts smeared by frost and grease. They read a line they'd memorized months ago.

"The only clearance still live on Anza's board belongs to a Shift 2 loader who never showed up for their shift. Name's Kael Renner. Plate's still green, but no body ever came to claim it."

"Kael Renner," Nour said. "You're sure?"

"Doan," Nour said. "Who else knows about Renner?"

"Nobody I trust," Doan said. "The roster's public, but the no-show rule isn't posted anywhere. I learned it the hard way when my own clearance went cold last winter."

"A no-show's name stays good until morning reconciliation," Doan said. "The desk hasn't wiped it yet because the board is frozen. You want to ride down-line under a live name, that's the one you use. But you use it before 08:00, because after reconciliation, the name goes dead and whoever wore it becomes a ghost with a warrant."

Doan sat back down on the ore stub and began lacing their down-line boots, stiff with old grease, the laces fused at the eyelets. They worked one knot loose, then another.

Behind them, the yard gate groaned on its hinge. Fenn's reclamation unit wasn't due until 04:40, but the bay clock read a little past two, and the warrant served at first light. Six hours, give or take.

"Six hours," Doan said. "Then the desk wipes the board, Renner's name goes cold, and we're all ghosts walking."

Miko walked the ore siding with three coast tickets folded inside her coat and the overlap log heavy in her other hand. The ticket window was a slot in corrugated metal, frost smeared across the glass like someone had spit on it and wiped with a sleeve. She slapped a ticket on the sill.

"One rider," she said. "Culvert Nine. Name Miko Takeda. Paid in full."

The clerk didn't touch it. He slid it back with two fingers. "Red plate," he said. "Desk isn't signing riders off a flagged node. Paper passage is worth nothing when the board won't take a name."

"The desk isn't reading my ticket. It's reading my money."

"It's not reading anything," the clerk said. "Anza's red. No carrier will sign a rider the desk is already watching. You want aboard, you need a live clearance. You don't have one."

Miko stared at him until he looked away. She opened the overlap log to the page Doan had dog-eared. Kael Renner, Shift 2, Bay 4, clearance green. A loader who never showed up. A name that stayed good until morning reconciliation.

"Change of plan," Miko said. "Rider name is Kael Renner."

The clerk typed. The terminal stayed dark, then flashed green. Then flashed green again.

"That name's already aboard," he said.

"Then I'm late for my own shift." Miko tapped the sill. "Print the slip."

The printer coughed. A rider slip came out, warm and curling at the edges. Miko folded it into her pocket with the tickets. The board box beside the gangplate chimed. Once. Then again.

A second tone. A double ping.

The red light above the platform stayed lit. The ghost train on the far track didn't move; its couplers cycled once and stopped, choked by Fenn's frozen ore chute. Miko was listed as Kael Renner, and she was also still listed as Miko Takeda somewhere on Anza's plate. One body, two names, until the morning count decided which one was real.

She didn't board. She turned back across the plate steel toward the ore stub, where Nour and Doan were stacking cases on the hand cart and Ospina held the chipped die in one pocket and a live stamp in the other. The double ping followed her like a borrower calling in a debt.

Miko shouldered past them and grabbed a handle on the cart. "I'm aboard under Renner," she said. "And still Takeda. The board just pinged itself into a knot. We push before the desk wakes up and figures out which of me to arrest."

Miko put her shoulder to the cart handle. The wheels crunched over plate steel grimy with oil and frost. Nour took the opposite side, Doan took the brake, and Ospina hung back at the rear corner with the chipped die in one pocket and a live stamp in the other. The cart groaned under eleven seals' worth of cargo that had left Anza and never arrived anywhere.

"We push before the desk wakes up," Miko said.

They did not board the ghost train. They pushed the cart away from the ore stub and onto the 7-K, seven kilometers of disused resupply road packed hard by snow and disuse. It was unlogged. It was unofficial. Doan led, limping on a wrist that had just come out of locker cord.

Post 71 squatted under a dead floodlight. Kass stood beside a ghost rig with its transponder removed, dark and cold on the siding. A folded dish antenna lay beside the cab, its mesh ribs collapsed into a square the size of a lunch tray. One shout flare stood in the dirt, unfired.

Kass looked up from the rig's breaker box. "You're late."

"We had to buy a body," Miko said. "Or two. I'm Renner and Takeda at the same time until breakfast."

"The board can't hold both," Kass said. "One of you is going to snap." They nodded at the cart. "That's the skim?"

"Eleven seals short," Nour said. "Fenn froze the ore chute, so we're taking it the long way."

Kass kicked the folded dish. "I came out here for a thread. One ghost rig logged at Kettering, badge 2241, deleted itself at 04:51. No alarm, no scrub line. I burned the last capacitor charge in this dead rig to make Teodoro read Culvert Nine off Nour's tally card, and now this rig won't transmit, won't receive, won't do anything but sit here and rust."

"So you're leaving it," Doan said.

"I'm leaving the dish," Kass said. "And the shout. One antenna, one signal, one chance to call down-line and warn someone we're coming. I'm not taking it. The thread is worth more than the antenna."

They straightened. "One of the four ghost rigs is running the ore line tonight. I saw it on the dead board before I killed the power. It's not stopping for people. It doesn't slow at relays. It doesn't answer channel hails."

Ospina shifted the die between pockets. "Then we're walking into the path of a train that won't see us."

"Not walking," Kass said. "Riding. If we catch it where the 7-K grades down to the ore stub, we can flag it the old way. Hand on the rail, body in the way. It won't stop for people, but it might stop for cargo."

Miko looked at the dark rail. "You want to play chicken with a ghost train."

"I want to get this cart to Culvert Nine before dawn," Kass said. "And before the reclamation unit comes out of Anza at 04:40. First light, the warrant serves. We don't have six hours."

Nour said, "Then we push."

They turned onto the 7-K. The road climbed under a sky going gray with pre-dawn, the snow slick under the wheels. Behind them, post 71 grew small. The dead rig stayed dark. The dish stayed folded. The shout stayed in the dirt.

Ahead, somewhere on the ore line, a rig that did not stop for people was coming their way, and they were pushing a hand cart full of unlisted cargo directly into its path.

The rail hummed under Miko's palms. Not much. Just a shiver. But it was there.

"Did you feel that?" she said.

Doan did not answer. They were already running beside the cart, breath white, eyes on the dark grade ahead.

The reclamation unit came through the gate at 04:12, twenty-eight minutes early and running dark. It was a low rig with a steel cage bolted to the bed, the kind the line kept for pulling listed cargo back into custody — a box with a hatch that latched from the outside, sized for a man who'd stopped being a man on the board and gone back to being freight. It didn't stop at the plate. It rolled up to the relay door and idled.

The rider came down with a tablet already lit. "Reclamation. Live hands claim on one Marlowe, no fixed node, entered ballast at Kettering Bay 4. Point me at the bunk."

"He's crew," Fenn said, meeting them on the step. The tally card rode sealed inside their coat. "Anza plate. Living crew, countersigned under live seal."

"Hands claim supersedes a countersign." The rider turned the tablet around so Fenn could read their own name back at them. "Reclamation doesn't weigh who signed for him. It weighs which claim is still open. This one's open. The bunk."

This was the shape of a clean morning, and Fenn could see it whole: point at the door, log the handover as cooperation, walk to the desk at 08:00 with a record you could eat off. All it cost was a man who'd already given his name once and would not get to give it twice.

Fenn took the grease pencil from behind their ear and wrote across the bunk door in block letters: *LINE-TRUST CUSTODY — F.* Under it, the hour.

"You can't claim him," the rider said.

"Line-trust officer takes a contested body into personal custody pending desk review. That's the rule you're standing in." Fenn capped the pencil. "My name on the door. My neck if he walks. Nine years I've kept this record spotless, and that's the first mark I've put on it. You want to be the reason I smudged it, say so on your tablet. Loud."

The rider looked at the name, then at Fenn, then killed the tablet. "Custody's your problem now. We log the block and roll. Desk lifts your custody, we come back with a warrant and a bigger cage."

"Log it," Fenn said. The unit backed out dark, the cage swinging empty on its mounts.

Inside, Marlowe had heard every word through the thin wall. The idling, the hatch, the word *ballast*. He knew what walking out would buy. He'd stand, cross to the cage, climb in, be cargo again — and the brown-out would lift, the compressor would come back up for Ivo, and Anza's red score would have its body and go quiet. Easy. He'd done harder things half-asleep.

He stayed on the cot.

"Teodoro." His voice was steadier than it had any right to be. "You want the numbers, take them now, while it's still coming back in one piece and not in pieces."

Teodoro pulled the stool to the cot. "Bay 4. Shift two."

"Three badges clocked live. Voss, 2209, ran the reseal. Me, 2231. And a third, 2244 — clocked in, clocked out clean forty minutes before the lid came down. Except I remember taped gloves on that lid, counting me down, and those gloves were still there after 2244 signed off." Marlowe's jaw worked. "So whoever counted me in wasn't on the roster when it counted. That's your other one. Find 2244, you find who held the lid."

Teodoro wrote it on his cuff in grease.

Across the relay, Rhea sat at Ivo's cot, bulb in her fist. Three pushes, watch the chest, stop. She didn't look up. "Somebody write down that the compressor eats a quarter every cycle," she said. "I'm tired of being the only one keeping count."

On the wall by the pump monitor, the old resupply loop ran its strip of moving ink, the disused line tracked node to node. The culvert totalizer ticked. Half a ration, logged at Culvert Nine, live, right now — somebody down there drawing while Anza starved.

And under the flow line, the movement trace lit a single dot on the 7-K. Between post 71 and the culvert. Already walking the crew's route. Ahead of the cart, and coming the other way.
